frame: Tully read this from an old fisherman's logbook. The Humbret is clinging to the mast.
text: We left the harbour at dawn, when the water was flat and grey, and for the first two hours nothing happened at all. Then the wind swung around to the south, and the sea woke up in a foul temper. It shoved the boat from one side, then slapped it from the other. Grey waves climbed over the front rail and spat cold water into our faces. Every time we turned for home, the sea seemed to block our way on purpose. My brother, who has fished these waters for thirty years, went very quiet and gripped the wheel with both hands. Nobody made jokes. Nobody even tried to eat the sandwiches. It took us six hours to get back to the harbour, a trip that usually takes two. When we finally tied up at the jetty, I sat down on a crate and didn't move for a long time. We didn't catch a single fish, and I have never been so glad to see dry land.

frame: The Soggy Biscuit's radio picked up this blog from a space scientist. The Humbret is listening carefully.
text: For six years, my team has driven a little rover called Pebble across the surface of Mars, sending it instructions from a control room on the other side of the solar system. Pebble was only built to last ninety days. Nobody told Pebble. When its left wheel jammed in year two, it taught itself to drive backwards, dragging the broken wheel behind it. When a dust storm blotted out the sun for a month, Pebble switched off everything except its heater and waited patiently in the dark, all on its own, until the sky cleared. Every evening, at the end of its work, it sent us a photo of the Martian sunset, as if it were saying goodnight to the people who built it. Last week, the dust finally won. Pebble's solar panels were too dirty to charge, and its last message reached us on Tuesday morning: a picture of a small grey rock, and the words BATTERY LOW. Half the control room cried. The other half pretended they had dust in their eyes. We still send Pebble a message every evening, just in case it wakes up. Its little wheel tracks are still there in the red dust, and they will be for a very long time.

options: A clumsy machine that was fun to laugh at.

text: The piano had stood in the corner of the Mangrove Point hall for nearly eighty years, and for most of that time nobody had played it. frame: Wren wrote this for the Mirage Mangroves rescue centre newsletter. The Humbret came along to watch.
text: After four months at the rescue centre, Crumpet the green turtle was finally ready to go home. She had come to us in winter, tangled in fishing line and far too thin, and it had taken weeks of care and a great many squid before she was strong enough to swim properly again. On release day, six of us carried her down to the beach in a padded crate, while a small crowd gathered on the sand. The morning was calm and bright. As we set the crate down at the edge of the water, the sea opened its arms to her. Gentle waves rolled up the sand, curled around her flippers and coaxed her forward, as if the whole sea had been waiting for her to come home. Crumpet paused for a moment and lifted her head. Then she pushed off into the shallows, and the water folded itself softly around her shell. A few seconds later, she surfaced once, took a breath and was gone. Nobody on the beach said anything for a while. Then the youngest volunteer, who had fed Crumpet every morning, burst into happy tears. We will miss her, but she is exactly where she belongs.

options: That the sea is her home and is welcoming her back.

That the sea is dangerous and might swallow her up.

text: Dear Gus, I hope life on the Soggy Biscuit is going well and that you are remembering to wash behind your ears. I am writing about the sock. You know the one. It is grey, it used to be white, and you hid it under your bed before you left for the summer, along with half a cheese sandwich. Well, on Thursday morning the sock crawled out from under your bed by itself, dragged itself down the hallway and begged me to wash it. It left a trail of something green on the carpet. The cat took one look at it and moved in with the neighbours, and she has not come back. Your dad tried to pick it up with the barbecue tongs, and the sock wriggled out of the tongs and refused to go in the bin. In the end, I put it in the washing machine on the hottest setting and washed it four times. It came out a lovely pale grey. I have put it in a sealed jar on your shelf, because I know how you feel about your collections. Please never do this again. Love, Mum. P.S. The cheese sandwich is still missing. If you know where it is, please tell me before the neighbours' cat finds it.
